summary.summary: Brent's 2024/25 outturn shows external borrowing up £85.8m (10.5%) to £900.0m, funding a capital programme that pushed the Loan CFR up £102.6m to £1,357.1m (General Fund £1,015.1m, HRA £342.0m). A £13.7m budget variance on capital financing costs (£41.5m actual against a £27.8m budget) was offset by a drawdown from capital reserves. The council has grown related-party lending to its wholly-owned housing companies — £182.4m to I4B Holdings Ltd and £33.8m to First Wave Housing — and holds £59.5m of LOBO loans, of which £35.0m face an interest-rate review in 2025/26.

signals.headline: External borrowing rose £85.8m (10.5%) to £900.0m in 2024/25, from £170.0m of new loans against £84.2m of repayments.
signals.why: A rapid, double-digit rise in the debt stock within a single year.

signals.headline: A £13.7m capital-financing budget variance (£41.5m actual vs £27.8m budget) was offset by drawing down capital reserves.
signals.why: Financing costs are already outrunning budget, absorbed by reserves rather than a revised budget.

signals.headline: £35.0m of the council's £59.5m LOBO book (5 loans) is due an interest-rate review in 2025/26.
signals.why: If a lender exercises its option the council's own option is to repay at par, which is what councils do: every LOBO call we hold — Kent, Tameside, Newcastle, York, Barnet, Brighton and Hove, Bristol — was repaid rather than accepted. So the exposure is finding £35.0m and replacing that funding at today's rates, not paying a higher rate on it.

signals.headline: Loans to Brent's wholly-owned companies stood at £182.4m to I4B Holdings Ltd and £33.8m to First Wave Housing at 31 March 2025, both secured on company property, plus a £36.4m equity stake in I4B.
signals.why: Sizeable related-party credit exposure sits alongside the headline treasury debt figures.

news_drafts.headline: Brent holds £39.5m of LOBO loans, with a £9.5m loan reaching an option date in December 2026
news_drafts.lead:
Brent Council has £39.5m of LOBO loans, a type of bank loan where the lender may, on set dates, propose a higher interest rate and the council may then repay the loan in full instead of accepting it. The mid-year treasury management report for the Audit and Standards Advisory Committee, which meets on 30 November, says one £9.5m loan reaches an option date in December 2026.

At 30 September 2026 the LOBO loans carried an average rate of 3.00%. They are one of six borrowing lines in total external debt of £1,081.1m, with net debt of £1,007.5m. The others include £443.7m of equal instalment principal loans and £415.9m of maturity loans from the Public Works Loan Board, the government's lending arm for councils. The report does not say what will happen at the December option date. It says the council will keep the LOBO portfolio under review and consider opportunities to repay or restructure it "to mitigate interest rate risk".

The council's liability benchmark, a chart councils must publish comparing the debt they hold with the debt they need, shows LOBO loans of £59.5m at 2025/26, £39.5m forecast for 2026/27, then £30.0m, £15.0m and £10.0m, reaching nil in 2030/31. The paper says the council uses the option date as the maturity date for its LOBO loans.

news_drafts.headline: Brent forecasts £20.8m schools-grant overspend for 2026/27, taking its deficit to about £41m
news_drafts.lead:
Brent forecasts a £20.8m overspend on its dedicated schools grant (DSG, the government grant that funds schools) for 2026/27, which the council's papers say would take the cumulative deficit to approximately £41m by 31 March 2027. The forecast, as at 26 September, sits almost entirely in high needs, the part of school funding for children with special educational needs and disabilities: £104.9m of spending against £84.1m of funding. The total adds the £20.2m deficit brought forward from 2025/26.

The budget had already planned a £14.9m overspend in high needs. The paper says the high needs allocation "did not increase at all" in 2026/27, while the number of education, health and care plans, the legal documents setting out a child's support, rose by 10.4% as of January 2026.

Brent submitted its SEND Reform Plan in June 2026 and has recently been told it is accepted for the High Needs Sustainability grant, which the paper says will cover 90% of the deficit to March 2026. The statutory override, a government rule that lets councils keep such a deficit off their main balance sheet, has been extended to March 2028. The paper says deficits arising in 2026/27 and 2027/28 have no confirmed funding, and that the Government has not said what funding will follow after 2028/29.

The first two phases of the council's SEND capital programme are expected to add over 594 specialist places by January 2030.
news_drafts.paper_title: 08. Update on DSG HNB and Brent's SEND Reform Plan

news_drafts.headline: Brent pension fund reports 113% funding level at 2025 valuation, up from 87% in 2022
news_drafts.lead:
Brent's pension fund is in surplus, with a funding level of 113% at its 2025 valuation, against 87% at the 2022 valuation. The figure appears in the risk register presented to the council's Pension Board on 5 November 2026.

The register reports the whole-fund valuation results, which were presented to the Pension Fund Sub-Committee in October 2025. It says: "the Brent Fund now maintains a 113% funding level and is in surplus, compared to 87% in the 2022 valuation". A funding level compares the fund's assets with the cost of the pensions it has promised to pay.

The paper also records that the fund's prudence level on the key discount rate assumption was increased to 80%. The discount rate is the rate used to turn future pension payments into a value today. The papers give no further detail on the surplus or on what it means for contributions.

findings.headline: Each 0.1% reduction in the target collection rate would add a budget gap of approximately £0.2m, and the paper cites £3.8m of savings already proposed for 2027/28
findings.detail: The paper says that if the long-term collection rate of 97.0% cannot be achieved for 2027/28, the resulting budget gap would need to be addressed, potentially with in-year savings beyond the £3.8m already proposed.
findings.matters: The sensitivity of the budget to each 0.1% of collection rate gives a finance director a direct measure of exposure, and the savings already proposed show the scale of the gap being planned for.
findings.figures: approximately £0.2m per 0.1% reduction in collection rate; £3.8m savings already proposed for 2027/28; 97.0% long-term collection rate
findings.quote: Each reduction of 0.1% in the target collection rate will result in a further budget gap of approximately £0.2m.

findings.headline: The Collection Fund reserve is limited to surpluses built up from tax base growth, and the paper says it cannot be relied on indefinitely
findings.detail: The paper states that the reserve is held to smooth Collection Fund deficits but is capped at the surpluses generated by tax base growth. It says the reserve cannot be relied on indefinitely, so any future deficit will affect future budgets.
findings.matters: A deficit-smoothing reserve with a defined cap is a constraint other councils with Collection Fund risk would want to understand when judging their own reserve adequacy.
findings.figures: no figures given for the reserve balance
findings.quote: this is limited to the amount of surpluses built up as a result of growth in the tax base and this cannot be relied on indefinitely

findings.headline: The £1.5m hardship fund is expected to be fully utilised during 2026/27
findings.detail: The paper says the fund earmarked to support residents in financial hardship is expected to be used in full during the year. No further detail is given on how it has been allocated.
findings.matters: A fully used hardship fund signals demand exceeding planned support, which is relevant to other councils assessing the cost of their own hardship provision.
findings.quote: The £1.5m hardship fund earmarked to support residents experiencing financial hardship is expected to be fully utilised during the year.

findings.headline: Single Person Discount awards cost £19m at the end of October 2026, an increase of approximately 6%, while the number of awards fell
findings.detail: The paper reports that awards fell from 37,624 in October 2025 to 36,807 in October 2026, and that SPD accounts are under ongoing review to identify changed circumstances.
findings.matters: Rising cost with falling award numbers points to a change in the value per award, which bears on the tax base and on how a council reviews discount eligibility.
findings.figures: £19m (October 2026, paper states 'just over £19m'); approximately 6% increase; 36,807 awards (October 2026); 37,624 awards (October 2025)

findings.headline: A further review of the Council Tax Support scheme may be warranted in 2027/28, with any changes from 1 April 2028
findings.detail: The paper says it is too early to fully assess the long-term effect of the 1 April 2025 changes, but that continued expenditure growth suggests a review may be needed. It notes schemes are typically reviewed every three to four years.
findings.matters: A council signalling a scheme review because of cost growth is a decision a finance director or lender would track for future tax base and budget effects.
findings.figures: 1 April 2028 (earliest implementation); three to four years (typical review cycle)
findings.quote: a further review of the scheme may be warranted in 2027/28, with any changes implemented from 1 April 2028.

daily_post.headline: Phase 1 and Phase 2 of the SEND capital programme are expected to add over 594 specialist places by January 2030
daily_post.lead: Capital that brings places in-borough is the lever for reducing independent placement costs, and a finance director elsewhere can compare the places-to-savings ratio with their own capital plans.
